claim: Malaria infection starts with injection of Plasmodium sporozoites by an Anopheles mosquito into the skin of the mammalian host.
source: Malaria infection starts with injection of Plasmodium sporozoites by an Anopheles mosquito into the skin of the mammalian host.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission.

claim: Sporozoites are carried by the blood flow to the liver after entering blood vessels.
source: Sporozoites are then carried by the blood flow to the liver, where they initiate a liver- and subsequently a blood-stage infection (Sinnis and Zavala, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sinnis and Zavala, 2012.

claim: Sporozoite motility is essential for exit from the dermis and sporozoite infectivity.
source: Sporozoite motility, a substrate-dependent gliding motility, is essential for the exit from the dermis, and as a result for sporozoite infectivity (Vanderberg and Frevert, 2004; Amino et al., 2006; Hellmann et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Sporozoites move at 1–3 μm/s.
source: In comparison to fast migrating mammalian cells, such as lymphocytes, which crawl at approximately 0.1 μm/s, sporozoites move at 1–3 μm/s (Amino et al., 2006; Hellmann et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lymphocytes crawl at approximately 0.1 μm/s.
source: In comparison to fast migrating mammalian cells, such as lymphocytes, which crawl at approximately 0.1 μm/s, sporozoites move at 1–3 μm/s (Amino et al., 2006; Hellmann et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fast migration is likely key for sporozoite infectivity given the energy cost of such remarkable speed.
source: Given the energy cost of such a remarkable speed, fast migration is likely key for sporozoite infectivity.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the energy cost of movement.

claim: Gliding speed is affected by the turnover of focal adhesion sites.
source: Gliding speed is affected by the turnover of focal adhesion sites (Münter et al., 2009), as well as by environmental obstacles present in the dermis (Hellmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Münter et al., 2009.

claim: Gliding speed is affected by environmental obstacles present in the dermis.
source: Gliding speed is affected by the turnover of focal adhesion sites (Münter et al., 2009), as well as by environmental obstacles present in the dermis (Hellmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hellmann et al., 2011.

claim: On two-dimensional substrates in vitro, salivary gland sporozoites glide in a circular pattern.
source: While on two-dimensional substrates in vitro, salivary gland sporozoites glide in a circular pattern.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sporozoite behavior in vitro.

claim: In the dermis, sporozoite circular motion is transformed to a complex non-linear path.
source: In the dermis, this motion is transformed to a complex non-linear path (Amino et al., 2006; Hellmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CSP has important roles for the exit of Plasmodium berghei sporozoites from the dermal inoculation site.
source: Recent work has shown that both the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) and the thrombospondin-related anonymous protein (TRAP) have important roles for the exit of Plasmodium berghei sporozoites from the dermal inoculation site (Coppi et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppi et al., 2011.

claim: TRAP has important roles for the exit of Plasmodium berghei sporozoites from the dermal inoculation site.
source: Recent work has shown that both the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) and the thrombospondin-related anonymous protein (TRAP) have important roles for the exit of Plasmodium berghei sporozoites from the dermal inoculation site (Coppi et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ejigiri et al., 2012.

claim: Proteolytic processing of CSP leads to removal of the N-terminus and exposure of a cell-adhesion domain.
source: Proteolytic processing of CSP leads to removal of the N-terminus and exposure of a cell-adhesion domain (Coppi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppi et al., 2011.

claim: CSΔN sporozoites display normal infectivity when inoculated intravenously.
source: Sporozoites expressing a mutant CSP which lacks the N-terminus (CSΔN), thus mimicking the proteolytically processed form of CSP, display normal infectivity when inoculated intravenously (Coppi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppi et al., 2011.

claim: When CSΔN sporozoites are injected intradermally, parasites are undetectable in the liver and exhibit a significant delay in the prepatency period.
source: However, when CSΔN sporozoites are injected intradermally, parasites are undetectable in the liver and exhibit a significant delay in the prepatency period, indicating that CSΔN parasites are impaired in their ability to exit the dermis (Coppi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppi et al., 2011.

claim: CSΔN parasites are impaired in their ability to exit the dermis.
source: However, when CSΔN sporozoites are injected intradermally, parasites are undetectable in the liver and exhibit a significant delay in the prepatency period, indicating that CSΔN parasites are impaired in their ability to exit the dermis (Coppi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppi et al., 2011 and logical inference from the data.

claim: CSΔN sporozoites show only a small reduction in gliding motility in vitro.
source: CSΔN sporozoites show only a small reduction in gliding motility in vitro (Coppi et al., 2011), suggesting that these mutant sporozoites have additional impairments in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppi et al., 2011.

claim: CSΔN sporozoites have additional impairments in vivo beyond reduced gliding motility.
source: CSΔN sporozoites show only a small reduction in gliding motility in vitro (Coppi et al., 2011), suggesting that these mutant sporozoites have additional impairments in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo phenotypes.

claim: TRAP-VAL parasites carry mutations in the putative rhomboid-cleavage site of TRAP.
source: Mutant TRAP-VAL parasites carry mutations in the putative rhomboid-cleavage site of TRAP and similar to the CSΔN mutant, they have a more dramatic reduction in their infectivity after intradermal inoculation, compared to intravenous inoculation (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ejigiri et al., 2012.

claim: TRAP-VAL parasites have a more dramatic reduction in their infectivity after intradermal inoculation compared to intravenous inoculation.
source: Mutant TRAP-VAL parasites carry mutations in the putative rhomboid-cleavage site of TRAP and similar to the CSΔN mutant, they have a more dramatic reduction in their infectivity after intradermal inoculation, compared to intravenous inoculation (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ejigiri et al., 2012.

claim: TRAP-VAL sporozoites display a significantly reduced gliding speed in vitro, moving at approximately 0.5 μm/s.
source: Unlike the CSΔN sporozoites, TRAP-VAL sporozoites display a significantly reduced gliding speed in vitro, moving at approximately 0.5 μm/s in vitro (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ejigiri et al., 2012.

claim: Sporozoite dispersal gradually decreases over the first 120 min after inoculation.
source: Reconstructed tracks were re-centered by plotting to a common origin (Figure 1A), which revealed a gradual decrease in parasite dispersal over the first 120 min after inoculation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Highest dispersals of sporozoites were seen within the first 15 min after intradermal inoculation.
source: Highest dispersals were seen within the first 15 min after intradermal inoculation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Over the 110 min following the first 15 min, parasite dispersal gradually decreases.
source: Over the following 110 min, parasite dispersal gradually decreases, which is reflected in a gradual reduction of the slope obtained from linear regression fitting of the MSD plot (Figure 1B, inset).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The migration of sporozoites is not well described by an ordinary random walk.
source: The distribution of this probability P(r) was plotted in a normalized histogram (Figure 1C), and it was found that the migration of sporozoites is not well described by an ordinary random walk.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing sporozoite displacement to Brownian walk.

claim: The probability of large displacements is much higher than would be expected for a Brownian walk.
source: In particular, the probability of large displacements is much higher than would be expected for a Brownian walk (Harris et al., 2012) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Harris et al., 2012.

claim: The apparent gliding speed of sporozoites does not change significantly until 60 min after inoculation.
source: While the ability of sporozoites to disperse decreases significantly after 20 min and further during the following 100 min, the apparent gliding speed does not change significantly until 60 min after inoculation (Figure 1D), which shows that the decrease in MSD is not merely a reflection of sporozoites moving more slowly.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The decrease in MSD is not merely a reflection of sporozoites moving more slowly.
source: While the ability of sporozoites to disperse decreases significantly after 20 min and further during the following 100 min, the apparent gliding speed does not change significantly until 60 min after inoculation (Figure 1D), which shows that the decrease in MSD is not merely a reflection of sporozoites moving more slowly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that speed remains constant while MSD decreases.

claim: Over time, an increasing number of parasites engage in continuous circular motility.
source: Over time, an increasing number of parasites engage in continuous circular motility (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At 20 min and 30 min after inoculation, approximately 22% and 36% of total sporozoites exhibit continuously circling motility.
source: While at early time points, this sporozoite behavior is seen less frequently, at 20 min and 30 min after inoculation, approximately 22% and 36% of total sporozoites exhibit continuously circling motility.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: At 20 and 30 min, the increased percentage of circling sporozoites is not the result of other motile sporozoites leaving the field, but rather an increase in the absolute number of sporozoites that are exclusively circling.
source: Importantly, at these time points the increased percentage of circling sporozoites is not the result of the other motile sporozoites leaving the field, but rather an increase in the absolute number of sporozoites that are exclusively circling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: By 60 and 120 min, there are 20 and 40% fewer sporozoites in the field, respectively.
source: However, by 60 and 120 min, there are 20 and 40% fewer sporozoites in the field, respectively, and an increased number of non-motile sporozoites.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: At 120 min almost all moving sporozoites are circling.
source: Thus, at 120 min almost all moving sporozoites are circling (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The straightness of sporozoite tracks gradually decreases over the first 120 min after inoculation.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, the straightness of sporozoite tracks gradually decreases over the first 120 min after inoculation with the most significant decrease seen beginning at 20 min after inoculation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The most significant decrease in track straightness is seen beginning at 20 min after inoculation.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, the straightness of sporozoite tracks gradually decreases over the first 120 min after inoculation with the most significant decrease seen beginning at 20 min after inoculation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Sporozoite motility changes over time such that after an initial phase of maximal dispersal, sporozoites move in more constrained circular paths.
source: These data suggest that sporozoite motility changes over time such that after an initial phase of maximal dispersal, sporozoites move in more constrained circular paths.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on MSD, speed, and track straightness.

claim: A similar change in sporozoite motility was seen after inoculation by a probing infected mosquito, with a significant drop in MSD 20 min after mosquito bite.
source: Of note, a similiar change in sporozoite motility was seen in data acquired from sporozoites imaged after inoculation by a probing infected mosquito, with a significant drop in MSD 20 min after mosquito bite and a concomitant increase in the number of sporozoites engaging in circular motility (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sporozoites entering lymphatic vessels in the skin do not travel beyond the draining lymph node and thus do not participate in liver stage infection.
source: Although it was initially postulated that sporozoites might also reach the liver via the lymphatic vessels, a previous study found that sporozoites entering lymphatic vessels in the skin do not travel beyond the draining lymph node, and thus do not participate in liver stage infection (Amino et al., 2006; Radtke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amino et al., 2006 and Radtke et al., 2015.

claim: CD31 is a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily and is present on the surface of endothelial cells of both lymphatics and blood vessels.
source: CD31 is a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily and is present on the surface of endothelial cells of both lymphatics and blood vessels, where it is a constituent of intercellular junctions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD31.

claim: It takes approximately 24 hr for intravenously inoculated antibody to get into the extravascular space and be taken up by lymphatic vessels.
source: However, as we performed our experiments within 2–3 hr of intravenous inoculation of anti-CD31, lymphatics were not labeled in our studies, since it takes ∼24 hr for intravenously inoculated antibody to get into the extravascular space and taken up by lymphatic vessels (Sarkisyan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarkisyan et al., 2012.

claim: Lymphatics were not labeled in the studies performed within 2-3 hr of intravenous inoculation of anti-CD31.
source: However, as we performed our experiments within 2–3 hr of intravenous inoculation of anti-CD31, lymphatics were not labeled in our studies, since it takes ∼24 hr for intravenously inoculated antibody to get into the extravascular space and taken up by lymphatic vessels (Sarkisyan et al., 2012). This was confirmed by labeling lymphatic vessels with antibodies against the lymphatic vessel endothelial receptor 1 (LYVE-1) (Kilarski et al., 2013), which in the time frame of our experiments revealed no co-localization with CD31 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarkisyan et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sporozoites do not immediately penetrate blood vessels after contacting them.
source: Surprisingly, sporozoites do not immediately penetrate blood vessels after contacting them.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Sporozoites move on and around vessels for significant periods of time.
source: Instead, they move on and around vessels for significant periods of time, frequently even detaching from vessels and moving back into avascular areas of the tissue (Figure 2A and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 2A and Video 2.

claim: Sporozoites spend on average 28% of their gliding time near or on vessels.
source: We quantified the time sporozoites spend in proximity to blood vessels and found that on average, sporozoites spend 28% of their gliding time near or on vessels, which in our 4-min videos correspond to over a minute of total gliding time.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from the study.

claim: The average apparent speed of gliding sporozoites decreases from 1.38 μm/s to 1.06 μm/s once they approach a blood vessel.
source: Analysis of the two tracking sets showed that compared to sporozoites gliding independently of CD31-labeled vessels, the average apparent speed of gliding sporozoites decreases once they approach a blood vessel from 1.38 μm/s to 1.06 μm/s, and this difference is highly significant (p value < 0.0001) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The displacement of sporozoites gliding on or in proximity to blood vessels is decreased compared to those in avascular tissue.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the displacement of sporozoites gliding on or in proximity to blood vessels is decreased, as is the slope obtained from linear regression fitting of the MSD plot (Figure 2C, inset).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority of sporozoite tracks that overlap with blood vessels describe trajectories that have a curvature of 0.125–0.2 μm−1, which equals the curvature of the circumference of dermal capillaries.
source: The analysis revealed that while avascular tracks have little curvature, most commonly 0.077–0.125 μm−1, the majority of sporozoite tracks that overlap with blood vessels describe trajectories that have a curvature of 0.125–0.2 μm−1, which, remarkably, equals the curvature of the circumference of dermal capillaries (Figure 2D) (Yen and Braverman, 1976; Braverman, 1997).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Yen and Braverman, 1976 and Braverman, 1997.

claim: Sporozoite motility can change in response to environmental signals encountered by the sporozoite.
source: These data demonstrate that sporozoite motility can change in response to environmental signals encountered by the sporozoite and suggest that sporozoites in the dermis exhibit two types of motility: 'avascular motility', which is defined by high speed and less confinement, leading to maximal displacements in avascular areas and a more constrained 'perivascular motility', which is observed once the parasite glides in proximity of a blood vessel.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in motility near blood vessels.

claim: Sporozoites in the dermis exhibit two types of motility: 'avascular motility' and 'perivascular motility'.
source: These data demonstrate that sporozoite motility can change in response to environmental signals encountered by the sporozoite and suggest that sporozoites in the dermis exhibit two types of motility: 'avascular motility', which is defined by high speed and less confinement, leading to maximal displacements in avascular areas and a more constrained 'perivascular motility', which is observed once the parasite glides in proximity of a blood vessel.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in motility patterns.

claim: At 10 min after injection, only 47% of CSΔN sporozoites are motile.
source: At 10 min after injection, only 47% of CSΔN sporozoites are motile, however, this number is stable over time and similar to wild-type control levels at 30 min.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: Only 40% and 20% of TRAP-VAL sporozoites are motile at 10 min and 30 min after inoculation, respectively.
source: The analysis of TRAP-VAL sporozoites showed that only 40% and 20% of the inoculated sporozoites are motile at 10 min and 30 min after inoculation, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CSΔN sporozoites move with 26%-reduced average speed of 1.14 μm/s compared to wild-type control sporozoites which move at 1.57 μm/s.
source: Compared to wild-type control sporozoites, which move with an average of 1.57 μm/s, CSΔN sporozoites move with 26%-reduced average speed of 1.14 μm/s (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At 10 min after inoculation, TRAP-VAL sporozoites glide with an average speed of 0.72 μm/s, which is a reduction of 54% compared to the wild-type control.
source: In contrast, at 10 min after inoculation, TRAP-VAL sporozoites glide much more slowly, with an average speed of 0.72 μm/s, which is a reduction of 54% compared to the wild-type control (Figure 3C) and this is further reduced to 0.42 μm/s at 30 min after inoculation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TRAP-VAL sporozoite speed is further reduced to 0.42 μm/s at 30 min after inoculation.
source: In contrast, at 10 min after inoculation, TRAP-VAL sporozoites glide much more slowly, with an average speed of 0.72 μm/s, which is a reduction of 54% compared to the wild-type control (Figure 3C) and this is further reduced to 0.42 μm/s at 30 min after inoculation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutant sporozoites disperse less than wild-type control parasites 10 min after intradermal inoculation.
source: In agreement with the reduction in gliding speed of the CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites in vivo, it became evident that 10 min after intradermal inoculation, both mutant sporozoites disperse less than wild-type control parasites, which was visualized by plotting reconstructed sporozoite trajectories to a common origin (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The slope of MSD for CSΔN sporozoites is reduced to 1190 compared to wild-type control sporozoites at 2370.
source: Compared to wild-type control sporozoites, slopeWT = 2370, the slope of mutant sporozoites is reduced to slopeCSΔN = 1190 and slopeTRAP-VAL = 740, resulting in a decrease of over 40% and 70% of final displacement of CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: The slope of MSD for TRAP-VAL sporozoites is reduced to 740 compared to wild-type control sporozoites at 2370.
source: Compared to wild-type control sporozoites, slopeWT = 2370, the slope of mutant sporozoites is reduced to slopeCSΔN = 1190 and slopeTRAP-VAL = 740, resulting in a decrease of over 40% and 70% of final displacement of CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites, respectively.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: CSΔN sporozoites spend significantly more time in association with dermal vascular endothelia compared to wild-type control sporozoites.
source: Unexpectedly, it was found that compared to wild-type control sporozoites, which spend 28% of their motile time gliding in close proximity to blood vessels, CSΔN sporozoites spend significantly more time in association with dermal vascular endothelia; an average of 40.7% of their motile time is spent close to blood vessels (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TRAP-VAL sporozoites spend the same proportion of their motile time gliding close to blood vessels as wild-type control parasites.
source: In contrast, TRAP-VAL sporozoites spend the same proportion of their motile time gliding close to blood vessels as wild-type control parasites (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Similar to wild-type control sporozoites, perivascular CSΔN tracks have a decreased MSD and gliding speed.
source: MSD analysis of the two tracking sets revealed that similar to wild-type control sporozoites, perivascular CSΔN tracks have a decreased MSD and gliding speed (Figure 5C,D), indicating that while CSΔN sporozoites spend more time gliding in proximity to vasculature, the switch from 'avascular' to 'perivascular motility' appears normal.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The switch from 'avascular' to 'perivascular motility' appears normal in CSΔN sporozoites.
source: MSD analysis of the two tracking sets revealed that similar to wild-type control sporozoites, perivascular CSΔN tracks have a decreased MSD and gliding speed (Figure 5C,D), indicating that while CSΔN sporozoites spend more time gliding in proximity to vasculature, the switch from 'avascular' to 'perivascular motility' appears normal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CSΔN sporozoites show similar changes in MSD and speed near vessels as wild-type.

claim: TRAP-VAL sporozoites exhibit differential 'avascular' and 'perivascular motility', although the differences in MSD and speed between these two types of tracks is less pronounced.
source: TRAP-VAL sporozoites also exhibit differential 'avascular' and 'perivascular motility', although the differences in MSD and speed between these two types of tracks is less pronounced (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: On average, in a 4-min video beginning at 10 min after inoculation, 2.38% of wild-type control sporozoites in the field of view enters the blood circulation.
source: On average, in a 4-min video beginning at 10 min after inoculation, 2.38% of wild-type control sporozoites in the field of view enters the blood circulation, and 2.06% of sporozoites enters the lymphatic system (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: On average, 2.06% of wild-type control sporozoites enters the lymphatic system in a 4-min video beginning at 10 min after inoculation.
source: On average, in a 4-min video beginning at 10 min after inoculation, 2.38% of wild-type control sporozoites in the field of view enters the blood circulation, and 2.06% of sporozoites enters the lymphatic system (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Blood vessel invasion of the CSΔN mutant is reduced to 0.23%.
source: Blood vessel invasion of the CSΔN mutant is reduced to 0.23% and only 0.05% of TRAP-VAL sporozoites is seen to enter into blood vessels (Figure 5E), which is consistent with the decrease in infectivity of these mutants upon intradermal inoculation (Coppi et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Only 0.05% of TRAP-VAL sporozoites is seen to enter into blood vessels.
source: Blood vessel invasion of the CSΔN mutant is reduced to 0.23% and only 0.05% of TRAP-VAL sporozoites is seen to enter into blood vessels (Figure 5E), which is consistent with the decrease in infectivity of these mutants upon intradermal inoculation (Coppi et al., 2011; Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Invasion of the lymphatic system by CSΔN sporozoites is reduced to 0.26%.
source: Invasion of the lymphatic system by CSΔN sporozoites is reduced to 0.26% and not detected at all in the case of TRAP-VAL sporozoites (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Lymphatic invasion by TRAP-VAL sporozoites was not detected.
source: Invasion of the lymphatic system by CSΔN sporozoites is reduced to 0.26% and not detected at all in the case of TRAP-VAL sporozoites (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CD31-labeling is not interfering with entry into dermal blood or lymphatic vessels or parasite dispersal.
source: Importantly, CD31-labeling is not interfering with entry into dermal blood or lymphatic vessels or parasite dispersal, as vessel invasion rates, as well as sporozoite MSDs, are comparable in videos acquired in mice with and without labeled blood vessels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRAP-VAL sporozoites spend on average 40% less time on vessels compared to wild-type control sporozoites.
source: As shown in Figure 5B (right panel), TRAP-VAL sporozoites spend on average, 40% less time on vessels compared to wild-type control sporozoites, a decrease that is due, in part, to the large number of non-motile TRAP-VAL sporozoites.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The population of TRAP-VAL sporozoites spends approximately 10% of its time on or near blood vessels.
source: Nonetheless, the population of TRAP-VAL sporozoites still spends approximately 10% of its time on or near blood vessels, yet blood vessel entry events were reduced by 97%, suggesting that even when TRAP-VAL sporozoites do contact vessels they cannot invade them.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: Even when TRAP-VAL sporozoites do contact vessels they cannot invade them.
source: Nonetheless, the population of TRAP-VAL sporozoites still spends approximately 10% of its time on or near blood vessels, yet blood vessel entry events were reduced by 97%, suggesting that even when TRAP-VAL sporozoites do contact vessels they cannot invade them.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between time spent on vessels and invasion rate.

claim: CSΔN sporozoites spend approximately the same total time on vessels as the control wild-type sporozoites, yet blood vessel entry events were reduced by 90%.
source: This is even more dramatically illustrated by the CSΔN mutant that spends approximately the same total time on vessels as the control wild-type sporozoites (Figure 5B, right panel), yet blood vessel entry events were reduced by 90%.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutations result in the increased surface exposure of cell-adhesion domains.
source: Indeed, both CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutations result in the increased surface exposure of cell-adhesion domains: in CSΔN sporozoites, the absence of the N-terminus leads to constitutive exposure of the cell-adhesive type I thrombospondin domain in the C-terminus of the protein (Coppi et al., 2011) and in TRAP-VAL sporozoites, the altered proteolytic cleavage site leads to the retention of TRAP molecules on the sporozoite's surface (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coppi et al., 2011 and Ejigiri et al., 2012.

claim: The inability of CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutants to regulate their adhesive interactions likely results in their inability to complete the entry process.
source: Thus, the inability of these mutants to regulate their adhesive interactions likely results in their inability to complete the entry process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants with increased adhesion cannot enter vessels.

claim: Within the first 20 min after intradermal inoculation, sporozoites displace with high speed and minimal constraint, which likely maximizes the volume of tissue that is explored by the population of sporozoites.
source: Within the first 20 min after intradermal inoculation, sporozoites displace with high speed and minimal constraint, which likely maximizes the volume of tissue that is explored by the population of sporozoites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed motility patterns.

claim: After the initial period of dispersal, sporozoite motility changes, with the migratory pattern becoming increasingly confined starting 20 min after inoculation.
source: After this initial period of dispersal, sporozoite motility changes. Most significantly starting 20 min after inoculation, the migratory pattern of sporozoites becomes increasingly confined, and a growing number of sporozoites engage in continuous circular motility.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: The motility pattern observed 20-30 min post-inoculation optimizes engagement with blood vessels that will ultimately lead to blood vessel entry.
source: We hypothesize that this motility pattern optimizes engagement with blood vessels that will ultimately lead to blood vessel entry.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed motility changes.

claim: 1 hr after inoculation, sporozoites begin to slow down and a significant proportion stop moving.
source: 1 hr after inoculation, sporozoites begin to slow down and a significant proportion stop moving with the proportion of non-motile sporozoites increasing to 70% by 2 hr.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: The proportion of non-motile sporozoites increases to 70% by 2 hr after inoculation.
source: 1 hr after inoculation, sporozoites begin to slow down and a significant proportion stop moving with the proportion of non-motile sporozoites increasing to 70% by 2 hr.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: The late-phase slow down at 60-120 min is distinct from the change in trajectory that occurs 20 and 30 min post inoculation.
source: Importantly, this late-phase slow down is distinct from the change in trajectory that occurs 20 and 30 min post inoculation when the speed and proportion of non-motile sporozoites does not change from what is observed at earlier time points.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the different time points.

claim: The larger than expected displacements may allow the sporozoite to cover large distances between the blood vessels, which may enable the sporozoite to encounter blood vessels with higher efficiency than Brownian random walkers.
source: The larger than expected displacements may allow the sporozoite to cover large distances between the blood vessels, which may enable the sporozoite to encounter blood vessels with higher efficiency than Brownian random walkers.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed displacement patterns.

claim: The switch in sporozoite motility near blood vessels points to a specific host–parasite interaction between the parasite and the environment of the blood vessel.
source: This points to a specific host–parasite interaction between the parasite and the environment of the blood vessel and provides evidence for the ability of the sporozoite to alter motility in response to host factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in motility near vessels.

claim: Sporozoites have been shown to respond to obstacle cues in micro-fabricated arrays in vitro.
source: Indeed, in vitro, sporozoites have been shown to respond to obstacle cues in micro-fabricated arrays so it is possible that environmental constraints alone account for the switch in the sporozoites' migration pattern (Hellmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hellmann et al., 2011.

claim: The observation that the sporozoites' walk statistics change in proximity to blood vessels indicates that there is a specific recognition event that leads to this change.
source: However, our observation that the sporozoites' walk statistics change in proximity to blood vessels indicates that there is a specific recognition event that leads to this change.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical changes observed near vessels.

claim: 'Perivascular motility' enhances contact with capillaries, rather than the larger dermal terminal arterioles or post-capillary venules.
source: This suggests that 'perivascular motility' enhances contact with capillaries, rather than the larger dermal terminal arterioles or post-capillary venules (Yen and Braverman, 1976; Braverman, 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the curvature analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The curvature of the sporozoite matches the geometry of capillaries.
source: Indeed, it has been observed previously, that the curvature of the sporozoite matches the geometry of capillaries (Vanderberg, 1974) and more recently, a study using stochastic computer simulations of sporozoite motility found that in these models, sporozoite interaction with capillaries is greatly enhanced if the parasite has the ability to adapt its curvature and torsion to the surrounding environment (Battista et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vanderberg, 1974 and Battista et al., 2014.

claim: The importance of high sporozoite gliding speed is highlighted by the behavior of the TRAP-VAL mutant.
source: The importance of high sporozoite gliding speed is highlighted by the behavior of the TRAP-VAL mutant that moves with less than half the motile speed of wild-type control parasites in the dermis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotype of TRAP-VAL mutants.

claim: The decrease in speed of TRAP-VAL sporozoites corresponds to a reduction of final MSD, which reduces the area of tissue explored by 70%.
source: This decrease in speed corresponds to the reduction of final MSD, which reduces the area of tissue explored by 70%.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: TRAP-VAL sporozoites have a significantly decreased chance to encounter and invade a blood vessel.
source: Consequently, TRAP-VAL sporozoites have a significantly decreased chance to encounter and invade a blood vessel, which together with the increase in number of non-motile TRAP-VAL sporozoites, largely explains their reduced infectivity (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced motility and supported by citation.

claim: The observed rapid dispersal of wild-type control sporozoites suggests that the parasite has evolved to leave the skin quickly, possibly as a means to escape from phagocytic host cells.
source: Although there is no evidence for an innate host immune response that may impair the exit of sporozoites from the dermis, the observed rapid dispersal of wild-type control sporozoites suggests that the parasite has evolved to leave the skin quickly, possibly as a means to escape from phagocytic host cells (Amino et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Amino et al., 2008.

claim: The constitutively exposed TSR on the surface of CSΔN sporozoites leads to increased time spent on vascular endothelia.
source: We find that the constitutively exposed TSR on the surface of CSΔN sporozoites leads to increased time spent on vascular endothelia.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: The ability of the sporozoite to dynamically regulate exposure of the TSR is necessary for continued migration through the dermis.
source: We therefore hypothesize that the ability of the sporozoite to dynamically regulate exposure of the TSR is necessary for continued migration through the dermis, which may be crucial for the sporozoite to locate the areas of the vasculature that allow for blood vessel entry or for blood vessel entry itself.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed behavior of CSΔN mutants.

claim: The sporozoite's ability to regulate its adhesive interactions is a key factor for successful movement through and out of the dermis.
source: More work is needed to determine if this is the case, however, our data with both TRAP-VAL and CSΔN mutant sporozoites demonstrate that the sporozoite's ability to regulate its adhesive intereactions is a key factor for successful movement through and out of the dermis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on both mutants.

claim: Wild-type control sporozoites spend over a quarter of their time engaging with blood vessels, frequently without successful entry into the blood circulation.
source: We show that wild-type control sporozoites spend over a quarter of their time engaging with blood vessels, frequently without successful entry into the blood circulation.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: Only certain areas of the vasculature are suitable for sporozoite entry.
source: This suggests that only certain areas of the vasculature are suitable for sporozoite entry.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sporozoites spend time on vessels without entering.

claim: The basement membrane surrounding the capillary bed is not continuous.
source: It is known that the abluminal surface of dermal capillaries is not uniform; for example, the basement membrane surrounding the capillary bed is not continuous and through its gaps, pericytes form tight junctions with the underlying endothelial cell (Braverman, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Braverman, 1997.

claim: There may be certain areas of the vasculature that are preferentially invaded by sporozoites.
source: Thus, there may be certain areas of the vasculature that are preferentially invaded by sporozoites.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the heterogeneity of the vasculature.

claim: Mutant sporozoites that display modest changes in motility pattern or speed have dramatic decreases in blood vessel invasion and infectivity.
source: Mutant sporozoites that display modest changes in motility pattern or speed have dramatic decreases in blood vessel invasion and infectivity.
evidence: Supported by data from the study.

claim: Exit from the inoculation site presents an important barrier for the sporozoite.
source: These data suggest that exit from the inoculation site presents an important barrier for the sporozoite and is therefore an opportune time to intervene.
evidence: This is inferred from the dramatic effects of modest motility changes.

claim: The partial success of RTS,S may result from antibodies that target sporozoites in the dermis.
source: Indeed, the partial success of RTS,S, the only malaria vaccine candidate in Phase III clinical trials, may result from antibodies that target sporozoites in the dermis (Foquet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Foquet et al., 2014.

claim: An analysis of dermal sporozoite motility could be incorporated in the evaluation of future vaccine strategies to predict efficiency of new vaccine targets.
source: Additionally, our data suggest that an analysis of dermal sporozoite motility could be incorporated in the evaluation of future vaccine strategies to predict efficiency of new vaccine targets.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the findings of the study.
